summary: Declares RFC 1264, which prescribed rules to protect the Internet from new routing protocols with undesirable properties, obsolete. The Internet now has many other pressures against deploying unreasonable protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo retires the general rules for publishing routing protocols in RFC 1264. It says the broader standards process already lets the IESG ask for implementation or operational experience when needed.

questions: why were routing protocol rules dropped
why were routing protocol rules retired
subtitle: Why the IETF reclassified its general routing protocol rules as Historic.

tldr.problem: RFC 1264 imposed extra requirements on routing protocols seeking the IETF Standards Track, and the memo says those rules slowed timely publication.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4794 reclassifies RFC 1264 as Historic while leaving the RFC 2026 standards process in place.
tldr.outcome: The broad requirement for all routing documents is removed, while routing working groups may keep their own procedures.

today: RFC 4794 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1264 by reclassifying it as Historic. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes RFC 4794.

sections.title: What RFC 1264 Required
sections.content:
RFC 1264 set rules for publishing routing protocols on the IETF Standards Track. These included requirements for implementation, management information bases and security. The rules aimed to protect the Internet from incomplete or unscalable protocols.

RFC 4794 says that additional rules for one class of protocols hurt the IETF's ability to publish specifications in a timely way.
sections.plainLanguage: An earlier RFC added special checks for routing protocols. This memo says those checks made it harder to publish documents on time.

sections.title: Why the Rules Were Retired
sections.content:
The standards process in RFC 2026 already permits the IESG to require implementation or operational experience when a specification affects core Internet protocols or could have significant operational impact.

This memo therefore reclassifies RFC 1264 as Historic and removes its broad requirement from all routing documents. The Routing Area Directors may still require experience under the RFC 2026 rules. Work to write a replacement set of rules was abandoned after public discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing process already lets the IESG ask for evidence when a protocol needs it. The extra rule for every routing document is no longer required.

sections.title: Working-Group Procedures and Manageability
sections.content:
Some Routing Area working groups had procedures based on RFC 1264, including requiring implementations before sending a document to the IESG. RFC 4794 does not prevent those groups from continuing their procedures and encourages groups to use measures that improve their work.

A management information base module is still encouraged in a broad sense, but it is not a limiting requirement. A manageability-requirements section should be considered but is not currently required. The memo says existing security policies, including a Security Considerations section, suffice.
sections.plainLanguage: Working groups may keep stricter checks they already use. Planning how a protocol will be managed is encouraged, but is not made a general requirement here.

references.text: Hinden, R., "Internet Engineering Task Force Internet Routing Protocol Standardization Criteria", RFC 1264, October 1991.
Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
